sentences.text: The name Lythronax combines Greek words meaning gore and king.
Its specific name, argestes, honors a southwest wind named by the ancient poet Homer.
This animal differed from most other tyrannosaurids by having a shortened skull with a broadened rear and forward-directed eye sockets.
The snout was comparatively short, making up less than two-thirds of the total skull length.
Lythronax possessed unique features for its time, including a short and narrow snout, a wide posterior skull, and forward-facing eyes.
The frontmost teeth were the largest, with the longest measuring almost 13 centimeters.
It is estimated to have been between 5 and 8 meters long and weighed between 0.5 and 2.5 tonnes.
Lythronax was likely the largest predator in its ecosystem.
It had strong bite forces capable of crushing bone, not just carving flesh.
The species was described by Loewen and colleagues in 2013.
The only known specimen was discovered in 2009 in the Wahweap Formation of the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in Utah.
Paleontologist Mark A. Loewen and colleagues designated specimen UMNH VP 20200 as the holotype for Lythronax argestes in 2013.
This holotype specimen was recovered from locality UMNH VP 1501 in the Wahweap Formation within the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Kane County, southern Utah.
Lythronax argestes is the oldest known tyrannosaurid based on its stratigraphic position.
Lythronax had forward-facing eyes that provided depth perception, likely useful for pursuit or ambush predation.
This skull anatomy would have given Lythronax binocular vision, allowing it to perceive depth, a condition considered predatory.
The discovery of Lythronax suggests that forward-directed orbits appeared in tyrannosauroids by at least 80 million years ago.
As a tyrannosaurid, Lythronax likely had a large body size, powerful jaw muscles, robust teeth, reinforced skull sutures, and small forelimbs.
It is suggested that Lythronax's teeth were used not only to cut meat but also to inflict damage and break bones.
The shape of its teeth would have made Lythronax an efficient hunter capable of tearing off huge chunks of meat and bone and swallowing them whole.
Vertebrates in the Lythronax habitat included freshwater fish, bowfins, rays, sharks, turtles like Compsemys, crocodilians, and lungfish.
Numerous mammals lived in the Lythronax region, including multituberculates, cladotherians, marsupials, and placental insectivores.
Lythronax belongs to the family Tyrannosauridae, which consists of large-bodied coelurosaurs.
Lythronax belongs to the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.
The species name of the animal is Lythronax argestes.
Lythronax lived during the Campanian stage in the Western Interior Basin.
The rocks containing Lythronax fossils are estimated to be 81.49 million years old, with an uncertainty range of 81.86 to 81.45 million years.
The environment where Lythronax lived included lakes, floodplains, and rivers that flowed east.
Lythronax lived approximately 80 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
Gregory S. Paul suggested that Lythronax argestes might belong to the genus Tyrannosaurus, arguing that derived tyrannosaurids are oversplit.
It is debated whether differences in phylogenetic results stem from an over-weighting of certain features by Loewen and colleagues.
It is debated whether Tyrannosaurus originated from Asian tyrannosaurids or from southern Laramidian tyrannosaurids.
